landing.title: How flooding looks across the Rio Grande Valley
landing.lede: One map to compare flood-hazard maps from FEMA, the State of Texas and local drainage districts, with documented floods, rainfall and flood-insurance claims alongside.
landing.feature.hazard.title: Hazard maps, side by side
landing.feature.hazard.text: FEMA's flood zones, the Texas Water Development Board's modeled floodplain and Hidalgo County's historic 1981 map, colored on one severe, moderate and light scale.
landing.feature.works.title: Drainage and flood works
landing.feature.works.text: Drainage channels, detention ponds, dams, levees, bridges, city storm sewers and bond-funded projects that shape where the water goes.
landing.feature.evidence.title: Evidence of flooding
landing.feature.evidence.text: Photos from the Hidalgo drainage district and FEMA, areas mapped as flooded in past storms, flood reports to the National Weather Service and insurance claims by census tract.
landing.feature.events.title: Floods and rain on record
landing.feature.events.text: NOAA's documented flood events since 1996, with the rain at the nearest gauges, and the wettest days ever recorded in each county.
landing.feature.claims.title: Claims and rainfall, year by year
landing.feature.claims.text: Flood-insurance claims, dollars paid and policies since 1978, set beside each year's rain and its wettest day.
landing.feature.alerts.title: Alerts as they are published
landing.feature.alerts.text: Current National Weather Service warnings, TxDOT road closures and Hidalgo County notices, shown just as each source publishes them.
landing.notice.title: Before you rely on it
landing.notice.text: This is a comparison tool for learning. It is not for emergency routing, flood-insurance or engineering decisions, and it does not show live flood depth. In a real flood, follow
landing.sources.title: Where the data comes from
landing.sources.text: FEMA, the Texas Water Development Board, NOAA, the National Weather Service, TxDOT, the U.S. Census Bureau, Hidalgo County Drainage District No. 1, Overture Maps and OpenStreetMap. Every layer names its publisher and its limits.

app.trends_title: Trends over time · RGV Flood Impact Visualizer
trends.no_rain: No rain gauge records for this county.
trends.tile.wettest_sub: {inches} in of rain, average of the complete gauges
trends.chart.nws: Flood reports to the National Weather Service
trends.note.rain: Average of the gauges that reported at least 330 days; a pale bar is a gauge year with too many days missing. NOAA GHCN-Daily.
trends.note.wettest: The wettest single day at any complete gauge. NOAA GHCN-Daily.
trends.note.over2: Days with more than 2 inches at a gauge, averaged over the complete gauges. NOAA GHCN-Daily.
trends.note.months: Average of the gauges that reported at least 25 days of the month; a month with fewer is left blank, not drawn as dry. NOAA GHCN-Daily.
trends.note.events: Flood-type events in NOAA's Storm Events Database, stacked by type.
trends.note.nws: Flooding reported to NWS Brownsville since 2005, stacked by kind.
trends.note.news: Each outlet's archive begins in a different year (Texas Public Radio 2004, Rio Grande Guardian 2006, ValleyCentral and The Monitor 2016, KRGV 2017), so early years are thin. Stories are matched by a water word and a Valley place; they are not verified conditions.
trends.claims_link: Flood insurance claims and policies, year by year, are on the claims page.

claims.notes.title: Where each column comes from
claims.notes.claims: Every flood-insurance claim FEMA lists for the county, counted by the year of the loss. Paid adds up the building, contents and compliance payments, as paid (not adjusted for inflation). Source:
claims.notes.rate: Claims for every 1,000 flood-insurance policies in force that year. Policy counts start in 2009; earlier years show a dash. Policies:
claims.notes.rain: Daily readings from NOAA rain gauges in the county. Rain is the average yearly total of the gauges that reported on at least 330 days; wettest day is the most any of them caught in one day. A dash means no gauge reported that often. Source:
claims.notes.rain_source: NOAA, Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (Climate Data Online)
claims.notes.event: The storm name FEMA gives the claims: the one the most claims carry that year. FEMA names only some claims, often a handful, so a blank doesn't mean there was no flood. Source:
